newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean traders shed light on Cargill failure.
newsitem.headline: South Korean traders shed light on Cargill failure.

text.p: A large consigment of zinc promised by North Korea to U.S. grains giant Cargill Inc under a landmark barter deal was sold instead to South Korea, metals dealers in Seoul said on Wednesday.
The dealers said three South Korean metals houses bought about 4,500 tonnes of zinc from the North in the weeks before Pyongyang cancelled the Cargill deal.

Under the swap arrangement, North Korea promised 4,000 tonnes of zinc worth $4 million in return for 20,000 tonnes of wheat with a similar value. North Korea is desperate for grain to stave off famine.

It had been widely believed that Pyongyang pulled out of the deal last week because it could not produce enough zinc, and this was seen as further evidence of the catastrophic condition of the North Korean economy.
But dealers in Seoul said the real story was more complicated.
Having struck a deal with Cargill to sell zinc at around $1,260 per tonne in early April, the world price of zinc rose sharply, and is now hovering at around $1,360.

Pyongyang decided to cash in at the higher price, and abandoned the Cargill deal with no explanation while the ship carrying the grain steamed in circles off the North Korean port of Nampo, the traders said.
"North Korea seemed to urgently need dollars and wanted to take advantage of high zinc prices," said a trader with a South Korean metals house that bought North Korean zinc.

Dealers said North Korea's failure to honour the Cargill contract still indicated it was chronically short of zinc. The country did not have enough stocks to both take advantage of rising world prices for zinc and keep on good terms with a potential long-term U.S. trading partner.
To facilitate the breakthrough swap deal, the U.S. government had offered Cargill a special exemption from a trade embargo with the Stalinist nation.
Sources said the three South Korean firms who bought the metal were LG International Corp, Tong Yang Global Corp and Taihan Suger Corp.
One trader said his company imported about 1,500 tonnes of zinc in mid-May, when three-month zinc prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) had reached their present level of about $1,360 a tonne.
The second company bought 1,500 tonnes at the end of May and the third purchased 1,500 tonnes in early June.

Traders said North Koreans preferred to do business with South Korean metals houses, which generally took a more understanding attitude to Pyongyang's erratic payment record. Several foreign companies have been burned in the past, and refuse to take any more chances.
One attraction of North Korean zinc in South Korea is that it is exempt from a three percent import tax. This makes up, to a degree, for its inferior quality.
Earlier, traders in Tokyo said North Korean zinc output was expected to continue sliding this year as the country struggled with serious shortages of electricity, ore and hard cash.
They estimated zinc production this year at well below the annual average of some 80,000 tonnes a few years ago.

North Korea's zinc sales to the South totalled 29,381 tonnes worth $30.7 million last year, South Korean figures show. The South has bought 6,505 tonnes worth $7.7 million in the first four months of this year against 6,499 tonnes worth $6.8 million a year ago.
